name: Medpor chin implant

lead: A Medpor chin implant adds chin projection to balance a recessed profile. It is a hard, slightly flexible porous polyethylene shaped to sit over the chin bone, and the added projection is visible once swelling settles.

Tissue grows into the implant's pores, which anchors it and supports blood supply. It is one of three common synthetic chin materials, alongside silicone and ePTFE. Published material is mostly technique descriptions; one plastic-surgery paper describes a modified, reshaped version for Asian patients. In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx option.

paras: A surgeon places a shaped implant over the chin bone through a small incision. Choice of material and shape is made with the surgeon, often compared with silicone and ePTFE. Swelling takes weeks to settle.

General chin-implant risks include swelling, hematoma, temporary numbness, infection, displacement and nerve damage. Because tissue grows into the pores, porous implants are harder to remove than smooth ones.

chain: Porous implant placed on chin bone
angle.text: A hard porous implant is placed over the chin bone to add projection and balance a recessed profile, with tissue growing into the pores to anchor it. The added projection is visible once healed. It is an established option, and published material is mostly technique descriptions.

lead: A Medpor chin implant is a chin augmentation implant made of high-density porous polyethylene, a hard, slightly flexible material. It adds forward projection and sometimes height to the chin to balance the nose and jawline in profile, and is often done together with rhinoplasty.[1] Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors the implant and supports blood supply, but also makes it harder to remove than non-porous alternatives.[1]

It is one of several alloplastic (synthetic) options alongside silicone and expanded PTFE, with bone-moving sliding genioplasty as the surgical alternative.[1][2] In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxxing option for chin projection.

A 2012 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper describes Medpor as effective for chin augmentation and recommends reshaping its outer aspect, particularly in Asian patients, to create an appropriate chin shape.[2] A 2025 systematic review of seven single-center studies (1,126 patients) compared chin implants with osseous genioplasty and judged both effective.[3]

paras: Commonly used chin implants are made of silicone, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) or high-density porous polyethylene (Medpor).[2] Wikipedia describes silicone as soft and flexible and easy to remove but able to shift, ePTFE as flexible and strong and usually fixed with titanium screws, and porous polyethylene as firm with tissue ingrowth that anchors it.[1]

The 2012 paper notes that it can be difficult to contour the inner aspect of the implant to conform to the patient's mandible, and that without modification a gap may result; it recommends modifying the external aspect, particularly in Asian patients.[2]

In sliding genioplasty a segment of the chin bone is cut, moved forward or back and fixed with plates and screws.[1] The 2025 systematic review reported higher infection and dehiscence rates for implants (up to 23.8 percent in the studies included), transient neurosensory changes with genioplasty, and better soft-tissue predictability with genioplasty (85 percent versus 66 percent).[3] A 2024 review of facial implant materials noted porous polyethylene had low infection rates and that no material was shown to be definitively superior.[4]

Risks listed in Wikipedia include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip weakness or numbness, and less commonly infection, implant displacement, bone changes and nerve damage, with surgeon experience lowering risk.[1] A 2022 case report described chronic infection requiring implant removal after years, caused by an exposed tooth root.[5]

Evidence consists of descriptive papers and reviews rather than randomised trials. One paper describes a modified Medpor technique for Asian patients,[2] a 2025 systematic review compared implants with osseous genioplasty,[3] and a 2024 review of facial implant materials called for larger randomised trials.[4]
